en: The Sūtra on the Meritorious Virtues of the Fundamental Vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was traveling through various countries for the sake of conversion and arrived at Vaiśālī.
In the city, he dwelt beneath a tree that produces delightful sounds.

Accompanied by a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus, thirty-six thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and an immeasurable multitude of others, he sat surrounded by them in respectful attendance as he preached the Dharma.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, bowed toward the Bhagavān with palms joined, and addressed him, saying: “Bhagavān!

I only pray that you will expound upon the names of such Buddhas as these, as well as their original great vows and sublime merits, so that all who hear them may have their karmic obstructions eliminated, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings during the period when the Semblance Dharma prevails.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

Mañjuśrī! Out of great compassion, you have exhorted me to speak of the names of the Buddhas and the merits of their original vows, for the sake of uprooting the afflictions of sentient beings entangled by karmic obstructions, and to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings during the period when the Semblance Dharma prevails.
"Listen now attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you. Mañjuśrī replied, "Yes, indeed!"
"We pray that you will speak; we delight in hearing it. The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"To the east, passing from here through as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Vaidūryanirmala (Pure Lapis Lazuli). There, the Buddha is named Bhaisajyaguruvaidūryaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān."

Mañjuśrī! When that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, he made twelve great vows to ensure that all sentient beings obtain whatever they seek.

"First Great Vow: May it be that when I attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi in a future life, my own body shall emit a blazing radiance that illuminates immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds; and with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary signs, may I adorn my body, so that all sentient beings may become no different from me."
"The second great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, my body shall be like lapis lazuli, transparent both within and without, pure and free from blemish; its radiance vast and expansive, its merit sublime; my body dwelling in perfect stability, adorned with a network of flames surpassing the sun and moon;
may all sentient beings in the dark realms receive illumination and clarity, and proceed according to their inclinations to perform all manner of deeds."
"The third great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, through immeasurable and boundless wisdom and skillful means, I shall cause all sentient beings to obtain inexhaustible objects of enjoyment, so that no living being shall ever lack anything."
"The fourth great vow:
May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, all sentient beings who practice deviant paths shall be caused to dwell securely within the path of Bodhi;
and those who practice the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas shall all be established in the Mahāyāna."
"The fifth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are immeasurable and boundless sentient beings who practice the pure conduct within my Dharma, may I cause them all to obtain unimpaired precepts and to be endowed with the three clusters of precepts."
Should there be any who have committed transgressions, upon hearing my name, they shall regain purity and not fall into the evil realms.
"The sixth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings whose bodies are inferior, whose faculties are incomplete, or who are ugly, dull-witted, blind, deaf, mute, dumb, crippled, lame, hunchbacked, afflicted with white leprosy, insanity, or various other sufferings of disease; may they all, upon hearing my name, have their physical defects and afflictions completely eliminated, and may they obtain a body that is perfect in its major and minor marks."
Upon hearing my name, may all attain physical beauty and wisdom;
may their sense faculties be complete and free from all illness and suffering.
"The seventh great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who are oppressed by various illnesses, having no refuge, no protector, no physician, no medicine, no relatives, and no home, and who suffer greatly from poverty—if my name should once reach their ears, may all their illnesses be completely eliminated, and they attain peace and happiness in body and mind; may their families and provisions all become abundant, until they even realize unexcelled Bodhi.

“Eighth Great Vow: May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are women who are oppressed by the hundred evils of womanhood and, having developed extreme weariness and detachment, wish to cast off their female bodies;
upon hearing my name, may they all transform from female to male, possess the marks of a man, and even go on to realize unsurpassed Bodhi.”
“The ninth great vow:
May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, I shall cause all sentient beings to escape the snares of Māra and be liberated from the entanglements of all non-Buddhist paths;

if they have fallen into the dense forest of various false views, I shall draw them in and establish them in right view, gradually leading them to practice the deeds of a Bodhisattva and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

"The tenth great vow: May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who are apprehended by royal law, bound, flogged, imprisoned, or subjected to execution, as well as other immeasurable calamities and humiliations, and who suffer physical and mental agony, oppressed by grief and sorrow— if they hear my name,
through the power of my merit and majestic spiritual authority, may they all be liberated from all their sorrows and sufferings."
"The eleventh great vow:
May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who, tormented by hunger and thirst, commit various evil deeds for the sake of seeking food;
upon hearing my name, they single-mindedly recite and uphold it, I shall first satisfy their bodies with the most excellent and sublime food and drink."
Thereafter, he establishes them in ultimate peace and happiness through the flavor of the Dharma. "The twelfth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who are poor and lack clothing, and are tormented day and night by mosquitoes, gadflies, cold, and heat; [may they all obtain exquisite garments, which are soft and pleasant to the touch, and may they never again suffer from such afflictions]."

If they hear my name and single-mindedly recollect and uphold it, they shall immediately obtain various kinds of exquisite garments, as well as all manner of precious ornaments, flower garlands, scented ointments, drums, music, and various performances—whatever their hearts desire for enjoyment—all of which shall be made fully satisfied.
“Mañjuśrī! These are the twelve sublime and supreme vows that the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, made while practicing the bodhisattva path.”

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! As for the great vows that the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, made while practicing the bodhisattva path, and the meritorious adornments of that buddha-field, I could not finish describing them even in one kalpa, or more than one kalpa.
Yet that buddha-land is uniformly pure; there are no women, nor are there any evil realms or sounds of suffering.
Its ground is made of lapis lazuli, its roads are demarcated by golden cords, and its cities, towers, palaces, pavilions, balconies, windows, and jeweled nets are all composed of the seven treasures.
Furthermore, its merit and adornments are equal and without distinction to those of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
Within that land, there are two Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas:

the first named Sunlight Pervading Illumination, and the second named Moonlight Pervading Illumination. They are the leaders of that immeasurable and innumerable assembly of bodhisattvas, and they are all capable of upholding the precious treasury of the True Dharma of the World-Honored One, Bhaisajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha Tathāgata.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī! All sons and daughters of good family who possess faith should aspire to be born in that Buddha-world.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī!

There are sentient beings who do not distinguish between good and evil, who harbor only greed and stinginess, and who do not understand giving or the karmic fruits of giving. Being foolish and lacking wisdom, they are deficient in the faculty of faith; they amass great stores of wealth and treasure, laboring diligently to guard them."

When they see a beggar approaching, their hearts are not glad; even when they are compelled to practice giving, it is as if they were cutting flesh from their own bodies, giving rise to deep pain and regret.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable sentient beings who are stingy and greedy, who amass wealth and property yet do not even enjoy it themselves, let alone give it to their parents, wives, children, slaves, servants, or those who come to beg.
When those sentient beings pass away from there, they are reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts or among the animals.

Because they once briefly heard the name of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha during their time as humans, even though they are now in the miserable realms, they briefly remember the name of that Tathāgata. At the very moment of recollection, they vanish from that place and are reborn among human beings. They attain the memory of their past lives, fear the suffering of the miserable realms, take no pleasure in sensual desires, and delight in practicing generosity. They praise those who give and have no greed or stinginess regarding anything they possess; gradually, they are even able to give their own heads, eyes, hands, feet, blood, flesh, and limbs to those who come seeking them, let alone other material wealth.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, there may be sentient beings who, although they have received the various precepts from the Tathāgata, violate their moral discipline (śīla);
or those who, while not violating their moral discipline, violate the rules of conduct (ācāra);
or those who, while remaining unbroken in both moral discipline and rules of conduct, nevertheless destroy right view."
There are those who, while not destroying right view, abandon extensive learning and are unable to comprehend the profound meaning of the sūtras spoken by the Buddha;

there are those who, though possessing extensive learning, harbor overweening pride (*adhimāna*), and because their minds are shrouded by such pride, they affirm themselves and disparage others, slandering the true Dharma and becoming partisans of Māra.
Such a foolish person, practicing false views themselves, further causes immeasurable koṭis of sentient beings to fall into great and perilous pits.
These sentient beings will thus wander endlessly through the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.

If one hears the name of this Bhaisajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabhāsa Tathāgata, one will immediately abandon evil conduct and cultivate all wholesome dharmas, thereby avoiding rebirth in the evil destinies. Even if there are those who cannot abandon evil conduct and practice wholesome dharmas, and thus fall into the evil destinies, by the power of that Tathāgata’s original vow, they shall temporarily hear his name before them; upon the end of their lives there, they will return to the human realm, attain right view and diligence, and skillfully harmonize their intentions. They will then be able to leave the household life for the homeless state, receive and uphold the precepts within the Dharma of the Tathāgata without transgression;

possessing right view and great learning, they will understand the profound meaning, be free from overweening pride, not slander the true Dharma, and not become companions of Māra. Gradually practicing the various bodhisattva deeds, they will swiftly attain perfection.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! If there are sentient beings who are stingy, greedy, and envious, praising themselves and disparaging others, they shall fall into the three evil realms and undergo intense suffering for immeasurable thousands of years.

Having undergone such intense suffering, when their lives there end, they will be reborn among humans as oxen, horses, camels, or donkeys, constantly subjected to whips and lashes, and tormented by hunger and thirst."
Furthermore, they constantly carry heavy burdens while traveling along the roads.
Even if they obtain human birth, they are born into low and base circumstances as servants or slaves, subjected to the驱使 (driving and service) of others, and are perpetually without autonomy.

If, in a previous human existence, one had heard the name of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, by virtue of this wholesome cause, one now recalls it again and takes refuge with a sincere heart.

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, they were liberated from all sufferings; their faculties became sharp and keen, and they possessed great wisdom and extensive learning. They constantly sought the supreme Dharma, always encountered virtuous friends, forever severed the snares of Māra, shattered the shell of ignorance, and dried up the river of afflictions. Thus, they were liberated from all birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! If there are sentient beings who delight in discord, who engage in mutual strife and litigation, and who disturb and harass themselves and others; who, through body, speech, and mind, create and increase various kinds of evil karma; and who constantly perform harmful acts toward one another, plotting to injure each other."
They summon deities dwelling in mountains, forests, trees, and burial mounds;
they kill various sentient beings, taking their flesh and blood to offer as sacrifices to yakṣas, rākṣasas, and other spirits;
they write down the names of their enemies and fashion their likenesses, cursing them with malevolent incantations.
Those who employ seductive charms and sorcery, or raise up corpse-demons through incantations to take another's life or destroy their body—
should any sentient beings hear the name of this Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, none of those evil deeds shall be able to harm them.
All, in turn, gave rise to minds of loving-kindness, seeking to benefit and bring peace and happiness to one another, free from any intent to harm or affliction, or any heart of resentment;
each was joyful and felt contentment with what they themselves received, refraining from mutual aggression while providing mutual benefit.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! If there are members of the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—as well as other sons and daughters of good family with pure faith—who are able to observe the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), whether for one year or for three months, and who, by means of these roots of goodness, aspire to be born in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss in the presence of Amitāyus Buddha to hear the True Dharma, yet whose destiny is not yet fixed; "

If one hears the name of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, at the time of death, eight bodhisattvas will come by means of their supernormal powers to show the way; one will then be spontaneously reborn by transformation amidst various multicolored flowers made of many jewels in that realm.
Some may, because of this, be born in the heavens; though born there, their original roots of goodness are not yet exhausted, and they shall no longer be reborn in any other evil realms.

When their lifespan in the heavens comes to an end, they are reborn in the human realm; some become universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) who govern the four continents, possessing sovereign majesty and power, and establish countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings in the ten paths of wholesome action;

others are born into great families of kṣatriyas, brahmins, or householders, abounding in wealth and treasures with overflowing storehouses, possessing handsome and dignified features, being fully endowed with kinsmen, and being intelligent, wise, courageous, and fierce like mighty warriors.
If it be a woman who hears the name of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru, and receives and upholds it with a sincere heart, she shall never again receive a female body hereafter.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

During the period when the Semblance Dharma prevails, I vow to employ various skillful means to cause all faithful sons and daughters of good family to hear the name of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, even so as to awaken their ears with the Buddha’s name while they are asleep.”
"Bhagavān! If one receives, upholds, reads, and recites this sutra, or further expounds and elucidates it for others;
whether copying it oneself or instructing others to copy it;"

With reverence and respect, they made offerings using various kinds of flowers, incense for anointing, powdered incense, burning incense, flower garlands, necklaces, banners, canopies, and musical performances;
they fashioned bags from five-colored silks to contain it,
swept and sprinkled a pure place, and prepared a high seat upon which to enshrine it.

At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, together with their retinues and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of other celestial hosts, all went to that place to make offerings and provide protection.
“World-Honored One!

Wherever this jewel of a sutra circulates, if there are those who can receive and uphold it, by virtue of the merit of the fundamental vows of the World-Honored One, Bhaisajyaguru-vaidūryaprabhāsa Tathāgata, and through hearing his name, you should know that in such places there shall be no more untimely deaths;
nor shall they have their vital essence stolen away by various evil spirits and ghosts.”
"If they have already been robbed, they shall regain them as before, and their bodies and minds will be peaceful and happy.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "It is so!"
So it is! It is just as you have said, Mañjuśrī!

If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who wish to make offerings to that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, they should first fashion an image of that Buddha and place it upon a pure seat.
They should scatter various flowers, burn various incenses, and adorn the site with various banners and streamers.

For seven days and seven nights, they should observe the eightfold precepts, eat pure food, bathe until they are fragrant and clean, and wear new, clean garments. They should give rise to a mind free from defilement and turbidity, a mind free from anger and malice, and toward all sentient beings, they should cultivate a mind of impartiality characterized by the desire for their benefit and happiness, as well as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. They should play music, sing praises, and circumambulate the Buddha image to the right.
Furthermore, one should mindfully recollect the merit of that Tathāgata’s original vows, read and recite this sutra, contemplate its meaning, and explain and reveal it to others.
Whatever one desires or aspires for shall all be fulfilled:

those who seek long life shall obtain long life; those who seek wealth and abundance shall obtain wealth and abundance; those who seek official rank shall obtain official rank; and those who seek sons or daughters shall obtain sons or daughters.
Furthermore, if there should be a person who suddenly has a bad dream, sees various ominous signs, or witnesses strange birds gathering, or if hundreds of portents appear at their dwelling;

if this person were to reverently make offerings with various exquisite requisites to that World-Honored One, the Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light Tathāgata, then all such bad dreams, evil omens, and inauspicious things will all vanish and disappear, unable to cause any harm.

Should there be fears of water, fire, blades, poison, precipices, or of evil elephants, lions, tigers, wolves, bears, brown bears, venomous snakes, malicious scorpions, centipedes, millipedes, mosquitoes, gadflies, and the like—
if one can with a sincere heart recollect that Buddha and pay him reverent homage, one shall be liberated from all such terrors.
If other nations invade and harass, or if thieves and bandits rise up in rebellion;
those who mindfully recollect and pay homage to that Tathāgata shall likewise all be liberated. "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who, for as long as they live, do not serve other deities, but instead single-mindedly take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts—whether the five precepts, the ten precepts, the four hundred bodhisattva precepts, the two hundred and fifty bhikṣu precepts, or the five hundred bhikṣuṇī precepts—and should they happen to violate any of those they have received, fearing they might fall into the evil destinies, if they can single-mindedly recite the name of that Buddha and reverently make offerings, they will certainly not undergo rebirth in the three evil realms.
If there are women who, when the time of childbirth approaches, undergo extreme suffering;
if they can with a sincere heart invoke the name of that Tathāgata, pay homage and praise him, and reverently make offerings to him, all their sufferings shall be eliminated.

The child born shall be complete in all physical faculties, with a handsome and upright appearance that brings joy to all who see him; he shall possess keen faculties and intelligence, live in peace and security with few ailments, and no non-human spirits shall be able to steal away his vital energy.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"The merits of that Buddha, the World-Honored One, Bhaisajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha Tathāgata, which I have thus extolled, constitute the profound sphere of practice of all Buddhas; they are difficult to comprehend. Do you believe this?"
Ānanda said: "O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!
Regarding the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, I harbor no doubt."
Why is this? Because there is no activity of body, speech, or mind of all Tathāgatas that is not completely pure,
World-Honored One!
These wheels of the sun and moon might be made to fall;
even Sumeru, the king of mountains, might be caused to tremble; yet that which the Buddhas have spoken shall never be otherwise.
“World-Honored One!
There are sentient beings who lack the faculty of faith; when they hear it said that the Buddhas possess such profound spheres of activity, they think to themselves:
‘How can one obtain such meritorious benefits and advantages merely by recollecting the name of a single Buddha, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha?’”
Due to this lack of faith, they instead give rise to slander;
throughout the long night, they lose great benefit and happiness, falling into the various evil destinies and wandering through saṃsāra without end.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“If these sentient beings hear the name of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, and receive and uphold it with a sincere heart, without giving rise to doubt or confusion, it is impossible for them to fall into the evil destinies.”
Ānanda! This is the profound sphere of activity of all Buddhas, difficult to believe and understand;
that you are now able to receive it, you should know that this is entirely due to the majestic power of the Tathāgata.
Ānanda! All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who have not yet ascended to the stages (bhūmi) are entirely unable to believe and understand this as it truly is;
the only exception being those bodhisattvas bound to only one more birth (ekajātipratibaddha).
Ānanda! A human body is difficult to obtain; within the Triple Gem, to have faith, reverence, and respect is likewise difficult to attain;
but to hear the name of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha, is even more difficult than that.
Ānanda! That Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha possesses immeasurable bodhisattva practices and immeasurable skillful means.
His vows are immeasurable and vast;

even if I were to explain them extensively for an eon, or for the remainder of an eon, the eon might quickly come to an end, yet the Buddha’s practices, vows, and skillful means would never be exhausted.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the assembly named Jue-duo (Trāṇamukta). He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, bowed with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Virtuous World-Honored One!..."

During the period when the Semblance Dharma prevails, there will be sentient beings who are beset by various afflictions; long afflicted by illness, they become emaciated and weak, unable to eat or drink, their throats and lips parched, seeing all directions as dark as the signs of death appear before them, while their parents, relatives, friends, and acquaintances weep as they surround them.
Yet that person’s own body remains lying in its original place, while they see the messengers of Yama leading their consciousness before the Dharma King Yama;
furthermore, every sentient being has a co-nascent deity who records all their deeds, whether sinful or meritorious, and delivers these complete records to the Dharma King Yama.
At that time, the king shall interrogate that person, calculate their deeds, and pass judgment according to their merits and transgressions.

At that moment, if the patient’s relatives and friends can take refuge in the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, invite the assembly of monks to recite this sutra, light seven-tiered lamps, and hang five-colored banners for the prolongation of life, there may be a place where that consciousness can return.
It is as if one were clearly seeing within a dream;

whether after seven days, twenty-one days, thirty-five days, or forty-nine days, when that consciousness returns, it is like awakening from a dream, and one fully remembers and knows the retributive fruits obtained from wholesome and unwholesome karmas.
Because they have personally witnessed the retribution of karmic results, they will not commit any evil deeds even at the cost of their lives.

Therefore, sons and daughters of noble family who possess pure faith should all uphold the name of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha and, according to their capacity, reverently make offerings to him.
At that time, Ānanda asked the Bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla:
"Good son, how should one reverently make offerings to the life-prolonging banners and lamps of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, and how should they be constructed?"
The Bodhisattva Trāṇamukta said: "Virtuous One!

If there is a sick person who wishes to be liberated from the suffering of illness, one should, for that person's sake, observe the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) for seven days and seven nights; and with food, drink, and other necessary provisions as far as one’s means allow, one should make offerings to the community of bhikṣus."
During the six periods of day and night, they should prostrate and make offerings to that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha;
recite this sutra forty-nine times;
and light forty-nine lamps.

One should fashion seven images of that Tathāgata, placing seven lamps before each image; each lamp should be as large as a chariot wheel, with their light remaining unextinguished for forty-nine days.
One should also fashion five-colored silk banners forty-nine spans long and release various kinds of sentient beings up to forty-nine times.
By doing so, one may transcend the perils of danger and distress, and shall not be seized by various calamitous or malevolent spirits.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

When calamities arise for a Kṣatriya king who has been consecrated by sprinkling—namely, the calamity of pestilence among the populace, the calamity of invasion by foreign nations, the calamity of rebellion within one's own realm, the calamity of portents in the stars and constellations, the calamity of eclipses of the sun and moon, the calamity of unseasonable wind and rain, or the calamity of drought when the time for rain has passed."
At that time, those Kṣatriya consecrated kings and others should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings, release those who are imprisoned,
and perform the aforementioned methods of offering to worship that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha.
By virtue of these roots of goodness and through the power of that Tathāgata’s original vow, his realm shall immediately attain peace and stability:
wind and rain shall fall in their proper seasons, the crops shall ripen,
and all sentient beings shall be free from illness and filled with joy.
Within that kingdom, there shall be no violent yakṣas or other deities who afflict sentient beings;
all evil omens shall immediately vanish;
and the life span, physical vigor, health, and sovereignty of the consecrated kṣatriya kings and others shall all increase.

Ānanda! If the Emperor, the Empress, the Queen, the Crown Prince, the princes, the great ministers, the high officials, the ladies of the inner court, the various officials, or the common people are afflicted by illness or other calamities and hardships, they should likewise erect five-colored divine banners, light lamps to maintain continuous illumination, release living beings, scatter flowers of various colors, and burn many kinds of famous incense; thus their illnesses will be cured and they shall be liberated from all hardships.
At that time, Ānanda asked the Bodhisattva Rescuer and Deliverer:
“Virtuous man! How can a life that has already been exhausted be increased?”
The Bodhisattva Trāṇamukta said: "Virtuous One!
Have you not heard the Tathāgata speak of the nine types of untimely death?"
"For this reason, I exhort you to create life-prolonging banners and lamps, and to cultivate various merits;
by virtue of cultivating merit, you shall exhaust your lifespan without undergoing suffering or affliction. Ānanda asked:
“What are the nine untimely deaths?
The Bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla replied:

“If there are sentient beings who fall ill, even though the illness is slight, they lack medicine and a caregiver; or even if they encounter a physician, he prescribes the wrong medicine. Thus, though they ought not to die, they meet with an untimely death.”

Furthermore, there are those who believe in worldly demons, external paths, and sorcerers who falsely proclaim calamities and blessings; they become terrified and shaken, their minds losing their rectitude. They resort to divination to seek out misfortune, slaughter various kinds of sentient beings, offer sacrifices to the spirits, and summon ghosts and goblins to pray for blessings and long life, yet in the end they cannot achieve it.

Thus, through foolishness and delusion, they believe in perverse and inverted views, which ultimately causes them to die an untimely death and enter hell from which there is no time of escape—this is called the first type of untimely death.
Second, they are suddenly executed by the laws of the king.
Third, through hunting and sporting, indulging in lust and craving alcohol, and being dissolute beyond measure, they are suddenly deprived of their vital energy by non-human beings.
Fourth, they are suddenly burned by fire.
Fifth, they are suddenly drowned by water.
Sixth, they are suddenly devoured by various kinds of predatory beasts.
Seventh, they fall precipitously from mountain cliffs.
Eighth, they are suddenly struck and harmed by poisons, malevolent incantations, curses, or the ghosts of the risen dead.
Ninth, being afflicted by hunger and thirst, one dies a sudden death because one cannot obtain food or drink.
These are the nine kinds of sudden deaths briefly explained by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable other untimely deaths that are difficult to describe in full. "Moreover, Ānanda,
King Yama presides over the records of the world’s registers."

If there are sentient beings who are unfilial and commit the five heinous crimes, who revile and disgrace the Triple Gem, who subvert the laws between ruler and subject, or who destroy faith and the precepts, the Dharma King Yama will examine and punish them according to the gravity of their offenses.

"Therefore, I now exhort all sentient beings to light lamps, fashion banners, release living beings, and cultivate merit, so that they may cross over suffering and calamity and not encounter various hardships.
At that time, there were twelve yakṣa generals in the assembly, sitting together in the gathering;
namely: General Piṅgala, General Vajrapāṇi, and so forth.
The Great General Micchila, the Great General Antira, the Great General Anira, the Great General Sandira,
the Great General Indara, and the Great General Pāyira.
The Great General Mahāpuruṣa, the Great General Candana, the Great General Kumbhīra,
and the Great General Vikarāla— these twelve yakṣa generals,
each with a retinue of seven thousand yakṣas, simultaneously raised their voices and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Having now received the power of the Buddha’s majesty, we have been able to hear the name of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha; from this point forward, we shall no longer have any fear of the evil realms.”

We shall lead one another, with a single mind, to take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha for as long as we live; we vow to bear the burden of all sentient beings, acting for their benefit, welfare, and peace and happiness.

In whatever village, city, town, or secluded forest there may be where this sutra is circulated, or where those who uphold the name of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha respectfully make offerings, we and our retinues shall protect such persons, causing them all to be liberated from every suffering and hardship;
and whatever aspirations they may have, we shall cause them all to be fulfilled.

Furthermore, those who suffer from illness or calamity and seek liberation should also recite this sutra; they should tie my name with threads of five colors, and once their wishes have been fulfilled, they may then untie the knots.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the yakṣa generals, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"O Great Yakṣa Generals!

If you wish to repay the kindness and virtue of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, you should always benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings in this manner."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what should this Dharma-gate be named?”
"How should we receive and uphold it?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This Dharma door is named 'The Exposition of the Merit of the Fundamental Vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha';"
It is also called the "Incantation of the Vow to Benefit Sentient Beings Spoken by the Twelve Divine Generals";
it is also called "The Uprooting of All Karmic Obstructions.
It should be upheld in this manner.

When the Bhagavat had spoken these words, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as the great śrāvakas, kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.

In the twelfth day of the fifteenth day of the second month of the second year of the Guangde era, the disciple Jia Chongjun resolved his mind to transcribe one fascicle of the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabhāsa-tathāgata-pūrvapraṇidhāna-guṇa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, praying for peace and security.
